claim: The activity of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting SARS-CoV-2 varies according to the variant of concern (VOC).
source: Recent in-vitro data have shown that the activity of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) varies according to the variant of concern (VOC).
evidence: This claim is supported by in-vitro data as indicated by the statement.

claim: No studies have compared the clinical efficacy of different mAbs against Omicron VOC prior to this study.
source: No studies have compared the clinical efficacy of different mAbs against Omicron VOC.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research, based on literature review.

claim: The MANTICO trial is a non-inferiority randomised controlled trial comparing bamlanivimab/etesevimab, casirivimab/imdevimab, and sotrovimab in outpatients aged 50 or older with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The MANTICO trial is a non-inferiority randomised controlled trial comparing the clinical efficacy of early treatments with bamlanivimab/etesevimab, casirivimab/imdevimab, and sotrovimab in outpatients aged 50 or older with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: This describes the trial design and is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Patient enrolment in the MANTICO trial was interrupted for possible futility after the onset of the Omicron wave.
source: As the patient enrolment was interrupted for possible futility after the onset of the Omicron wave, the analysis was performed according to the SARS-CoV-2 VOC.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the trial conduct.

claim: Among 141 patients infected with Delta, no COVID-19 progression was recorded.
source: Among 141 patients infected with Delta, no COVID-19 progression was recorded, and the time to symptom resolution did not differ significantly between treatment groups (Log-rank Chi-square 0.22, p 0.90).
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial data.

claim: The time to symptom resolution did not differ significantly between treatment groups in Delta-infected patients.
source: Among 141 patients infected with Delta, no COVID-19 progression was recorded, and the time to symptom resolution did not differ significantly between treatment groups (Log-rank Chi-square 0.22, p 0.90).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of trial data (Log-rank test).

claim: Among 170 patients infected with Omicron, 80.6% had BA.1 and 19.4% had BA.1.1 lineages.
source: Among 170 patients infected with Omicron (80.6% BA.1 and 19.4% BA.1.1), two COVID-19 progressions were recorded, both in the bamlanivimab/etesevimab group
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from viral sequencing data.

claim: Two COVID-19 progressions were recorded in Omicron-infected patients, both in the bamlanivimab/etesevimab group.
source: Among 170 patients infected with Omicron (80.6% BA.1 and 19.4% BA.1.1), two COVID-19 progressions were recorded, both in the bamlanivimab/etesevimab group
evidence: This is a primary outcome result from the trial.

claim: In Omicron-infected patients, the median time to symptom resolution was 5 days shorter in the sotrovimab group compared with the bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab groups.
source: the median time to symptom resolution was 5 days shorter in the sotrovimab group compared with the bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab groups (HR 0.53 and HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.36–0.77 and 95% CI 0.30–0.67, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis with hazard ratios and confidence intervals.

claim: Early treatment with sotrovimab reduces the time to recovery compared with casirivimab/imdevimab and bamlanivimab/etesevimab in adult outpatients with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection due to Omicron BA.1 and BA.1.1.
source: Our data suggest that, among adult outpatients with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 infection due to Omicron BA.1 and BA.1.1, early treatment with sotrovimab reduces the time to recovery compared with casirivimab/imdevimab and bamlanivimab/etesevimab.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trial results.

claim: Early treatment with casirivimab/imdevimab may maintain a role in preventing COVID-19 progression in Omicron-infected patients.
source: In the same population, early treatment with casirivimab/imdevimab may maintain a role in preventing COVID-19 progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of progression events in the casirivimab/imdevimab group.

claim: The generalisability of trial results is substantially limited by the early discontinuation of the trial.
source: The generalisability of trial results is substantially limited by the early discontinuation of the trial and firm conclusions cannot be drawn.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: A high incidence of hospitalisation and death due to COVID-19 has been reported among older patients and those with certain coexisting conditions.
source: A high incidence of hospitalisation and death due to COVID-19 has been reported among older patients and those with certain coexisting conditions, such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic kidney disease (Petrilli et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The implementation of mass vaccination campaigns has markedly reduced the healthcare burden related to COVID-19.
source: The implementation of mass vaccination campaigns has markedly reduced the healthcare burden related to COVID-19.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge and observation.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates differ considerably across countries.
source: Nevertheless, SARS-CoV-2 vaccination rates differ considerably across countries
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of global vaccination data.

claim: Growing evidence suggests a reduced efficacy of vaccines against new viral variants of concern.
source: growing evidence suggests a reduced efficacy of vaccines against new viral variants of concern (VOC) (Cao et al., 2022; Planas et al., 2022; Dejnirattisai et al., 2022; Andrews et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Neutralising monoclonal antibodies target the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 that mediates viral entry into host cells.
source: Neutralising monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) target the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 that mediates viral entry into host cells (Benton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Drug regulatory authorities granted emergency use authorisation for bamlanivimab/etesevimab, casirivimab/imdevimab, and sotrovimab based on randomised placebo-controlled trials showing efficacy in preventing COVID-19 progression.
source: Based on the results of randomised placebo-controlled trials showing the efficacy in preventing COVID-19 progression, drug regulatory authorities, such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the European Medicines Agency, and the Italian Medicines Agency (AIFA), had granted the emergency use authorisation status for bamlanivimab 700 mg combined with etesevimab 1400 mg, casirivimab 600 mg combined with imdevimab 600 mg, and sotrovimab 500 mg to treat early COVID-19 in patients at high risk of progression (Dougan et al., 2021; Weinreich et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the relevant trials.

claim: Two randomised trials have compared the clinical outcomes of mAbs in preventing severe COVID-19, showing similar effectiveness of bamlanivimab/etesevimab vs casirivimab/imdevimab in patients infected with the alpha VOC.
source: To date, two randomised trials have compared the clinical outcomes of these mAbs in preventing severe COVID-19, showing similar effectiveness of bamlanivimab/etesevimab vs casirivimab/imdevimab in patients infected with the alpha VOC (McCreary et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior trial.

claim: A randomised trial showed similar effectiveness of casirivimab/imdevimab vs sotrovimab in patients infected with the Delta VOC.
source: casirivimab/imdevimab vs sotrovimab in patients infected with the Delta VOC, respectively (Huang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior trial.

claim: Patient enrolment in the MANTICO trial started in December 2021.
source: The patient enrolment started in December 2021
evidence: This is a factual statement about trial timeline.

claim: Patient enrolment was interrupted after the publication of in-vitro evidence that bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab were not effective against Omicron VOC.
source: The patient enrolment started in December 2021 and was interrupted after the publication of in-vitro evidence that two treatments under investigation (bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab) were not effective against the new emerging viral Omicron VOC (Cao et al., 2022; Planas et al., 2022; Dejnirattisai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in-vitro studies.

claim: The analysis was restricted to 319 randomised patients enrolled up to the interruption for possible futility.
source: The analysis is therefore restricted to 319 randomised patients, who were enrolled up to the interruption for possible futility, and was performed according to the SARS-CoV-2 VOC (Delta and Omicron).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study sample.

claim: Eligible subjects were outpatients aged 50 years or older with a positive SARS-CoV-2 test and mild-to-moderate COVID-19 symptoms within 4 days of onset.
source: Eligible subjects were outpatients aged 50 years or older, presenting at three trial sites in Italy (Verona, Padua, and Udine) with a positive test (either direct antigen or nucleic acid SARS-CoV-2) and mild-to-moderate COVID-19 symptoms within 4 days of the onset (COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel, 2019).
evidence: This describes the trial inclusion criteria.

claim: Sample-size estimation was based on a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial assessing casirivimab/imdevimab efficacy.
source: Sample-size estimation was based on the only available double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial assessing the clinical efficacy of casirivimab/imdevimab (reference standard) in preventing COVID-19 progression in adult outpatients with early mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 (Weinreich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the reference trial.

claim: In the reference trial, hospitalisation related to COVID-19 or all-cause mortality occurred in 1.0% of patients in the casirivimab/imdevimab 1200 mg group and 3.2% in the placebo group.
source: This study showed that the hospitalisation related to COVID-19 or all-cause mortality occurred in 7 of 736 patients in the casirivimab/imdevimab 1200 mg group (1.0%) and in 24 of 748 patients in the placebo group (3.2%) (relative risk reduction, 70.4%; Weinreich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is data from a cited trial.

claim: 420 patients per group were needed to achieve 90% power with a one-sided α level of .025, allowing for 5% dropout.
source: Using these parameters, 420 patients per group were needed to achieve 90% power with a one-sided α level of.025, allowing for 5% dropout.
evidence: This is a sample size calculation based on statistical parameters.

claim: Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive bamlanivimab/etesevimab, sotrovimab, or casirivimab/imdevimab.
source: Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 ratio to receive a single intravenous infusion over a period of 1 hr, consisting of a combination of 700 mg of bamlanivimab and 1400 mg of etesevimab or 500 mg of sotrovimab or a combination of 600 mg of casirivimab and 600 mg of imdevimab.
evidence: This describes the trial randomisation scheme.

claim: Patients were masked to treatment group assignment.
source: Patients were masked to treatment group assignment.
evidence: This describes the blinding procedure.

claim: Randomisation was computer generated in permuted blocks with stratification based on site.
source: Randomisation was computer generated in permuted blocks with a stratification based on site.
evidence: This describes the randomisation method.

claim: The composite primary outcome was COVID-19 progression, defined as hospitalisation, need of supplemental oxygen therapy, or death from any cause through day 14.
source: The composite primary outcome was the COVID-19 progression, defined as hospitalisation, need of supplemental oxygen therapy, or death from any cause through day 14.
evidence: This defines the primary endpoint of the trial.

claim: Prespecified secondary outcomes included emergency department visits through day 28, all-cause mortality through day 28, duration of supplemental oxygen therapy, rate and duration of non-invasive ventilation and mechanical ventilation, and time to sustained patient-reported symptom resolution.
source: Prespecified secondary outcomes were emergency department visits through day 28, all-cause mortality through day 28, duration of supplemental oxygen therapy, rate and duration of non-invasive ventilation and mechanical ventilation, and time to sustained patient-reported symptom resolution, which was defined as the absence of any symptom related to COVID-19 for at least 24 hr (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Food and Drug Administration, 2022b).
evidence: This defines the secondary endpoints of the trial.

claim: Overall, 319 patients underwent randomisation by 20 January 2022.
source: Overall, 319 patients underwent randomisation by 20 January 2022 and were assigned to receive bamlanivimab/etesevimab (106 patients), sotrovimab (107 patients), or casirivimab/imdevimab (106 patients).
evidence: This is a factual statement about trial enrollment.

claim: No patients reported previous SARS-CoV-2 infections.
source: No patients reported previous SARS-CoV-2 infections.
evidence: This is a baseline characteristic of the study population.

claim: No patients were lost to follow-up.
source: No patients were lost to follow-up.
evidence: This is a statement about trial completion.

source: VOC data were available for 311 patients: 170 (53.3%) were infected with Omicron and 141 (44.2%) with Delta.

source: Serological positivity to anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies (p<0.001) and complete primary COVID-19 vaccination series within 120 days of the enrolment or booster vaccination (p<0.001) were significantly more frequent among patients infected with Omicron.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison.

source: No predictors were associated with the time to symptom resolution in both SARS-CoV-2 VOC.

claim: Cox regression analysis confirmed significantly different effects upon time to symptom resolution between sotrovimab and bamlanivimab/etesevimab in Omicron-infected patients (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.36–0.77, p 0.001).
source: The Cox regression analysis confirmed the significantly different effects upon the time to symptom resolution between sotrovimab and both bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab (HR 0.53 and HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.36–0.77 and 95% CI 0.30–0.67, p 0.001 and 0.0001, respectively).

claim: Cox regression analysis confirmed significantly different effects upon time to symptom resolution between sotrovimab and casirivimab/imdevimab in Omicron-infected patients (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.30–0.67, p 0.0001).
source: The Cox regression analysis confirmed the significantly different effects upon the time to symptom resolution between sotrovimab and both bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab (HR 0.53 and HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.36–0.77 and 95% CI 0.30–0.67, p 0.001 and 0.0001, respectively).

evidence: This is supported by subgroup analysis presented in Table 7.

claim: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, the paradigm of discovering and implementing mAb and antiviral treatments based on randomised controlled trials has lagged significantly behind new evidence from in-vitro studies.
source: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, the paradigm of discovering and implementing mAb and antiviral treatments based on randomised controlled trials has lagged significantly behind the new evidence coming from in-vitro studies, which has driven clinical recommendations causing ethical dilemmas on the continuation of ongoing trials.
evidence: This is an observation about the research landscape.

claim: Preliminary in-vitro studies on Omicron demonstrated numerous mutations in the gene encoding the spike protein, predicting markedly reduced susceptibility to bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab.
source: Preliminary in-vitro studies on Omicron demonstrated numerous mutations in the gene encoding the spike protein, predicting a markedly reduced susceptibility to bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab (Cao et al., 2022; Planas et al., 2022; Dejnirattisai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in-vitro studies.

claim: FDA and AIFA revised the emergency use authorisation for bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab, halting their use, following in-vitro findings on Omicron.
source: According to these findings, FDA and AIFA have revised the emergency use authorisation for bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab, halting their use
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory actions.

claim: The National Institutes of Health COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel advised against the use of bamlanivimab/etesevimab and casirivimab/imdevimab due to reduced activity against Omicron.
source: in line with the National Institutes of Health COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel, which advised against the use of these mAbs due to reduced activity against Omicron and because real-time testing to identify rare, non-Omicron variants is not readily available (National Institutes of Health, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to NIH guidelines.

claim: The study enrolment was prematurely discontinued for possible futility after inclusion of barely one fourth of the predefined sample size (1260 patients).
source: Therefore, the study enrolment in a real-life outpatient setting was prematurely discontinued for possible futility, after the inclusion of barely one fourth of the predefined sample size (1260 patients).

source: Overall, the three treatment groups appeared to be balanced with respect to the predictors of outcomes in both Delta and Omicron population, as expected under the randomised allocation design.

claim: Omicron is better equipped than Delta to infect people with pre-existing immunity.

evidence: This is a comparison of observed vs. expected outcome rates.

claim: The overestimation of the primary outcome could be influenced by the lower intrinsic-severity of Omicron, the high vaccination rate in Italy, and the prioritisation of booster vaccination for the elderly.
source: This overestimation of the primary outcome could be influenced by the lower intrinsic-severity of Omicron, the high vaccination rate in Italy, and the prioritisation of the booster vaccination for the elderly (Bhattacharyya and Hanage, 2022).

claim: A limitation of this study is the lack of data on the clinical efficacy of the study mAbs against currently circulating VOC (BA.2 subvariants, BA.4, or BA.5).
source: Another limitation of this study is the lack of data on the clinical efficacy of the study mAbs, as well as other commercially available early COVID-19 treatments (mAbs, such as tixagevimab/cilgavimab and bebtelovimab, and antiviral drugs, such as remdesivir, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and molnupiravir), against the currently circulating VOC (BA.2 subvariants, BA.4, or BA.5; CoVariants, 2022).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: The MANTICO trial is actively recruiting to compare the clinical efficacy of commercially available early COVID-19 treatments against currently circulating VOC.

claim: Additional clinical studies with adequate sample size are required to determine whether casirivimab/imdevimab and sotrovimab are effective in preventing COVID-19 progression due to Omicron infection.
source: Additional clinical studies with an adequate sample size are required to determine whether casirivimab/imdevimab and sotrovimab are indeed effective in preventing COVID-19 progression due to Omicron infection.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on study limitations.

claim: If the role of casirivimab/imdevimab in preventing severe COVID-19 due to Omicron infections is confirmed, this mAb could represent a readily available and well-tolerated treatment option in case of shortages of mAbs supplies and contraindication to other early COVID-19 treatments.
source: Should the role of casirivimab/imdevimab in preventing severe COVID-19 due to Omicron infections be confirmed, this mAb could represent a readily available and well-tolerated treatment option in case of shortages of mAbs supplies and contraindication to other early COVID-19 treatments.
